en: If the training consisting of the *keśavī*, *padī*, and *ātmikā* [recitations] involves an udātta following an anudātta and is followed by a svarita,
one should undoubtedly place the hand upon the heart, the head, and the root of the ear.
If there is an udātta following an anudātta and likewise followed by an anudātta,
one should place the anudātta in the heart and place the udātta on the left eyebrow;
then one should place it back in the heart— not higher— such is the established rule of the scriptures.
In the case of a combined pronunciation (*pracitoccāraṇa*), the placement of the hand is before the tip of the nose (3).

[The eight types of *krama* are: the natural (*jātya*), the abhinihita, the *kṣaipra*, the *praśliṣṭa*, the *vyañjana*, the *tiras*, the *tairovirāma*, the *pādavṛtta*, and the *tāthābhāvya* as the eighth (4).
The lords of sages, the Kātyāyanas, have declared the characteristics of these [four]; therein, regarding the four designations beginning with birth (jāti),
the wise one should move his limbs horizontally, just as in the rite for the ancestors (pitṛdāna).
If the accent is acute (udātta) like that of the word *manuṣya-dāna*,

then there is the pronunciation of *j* for a letter situated at the beginning or end [of a word], as well as for one read at the beginning of a word; however, in the Veda, this is not desired when it follows a prefix (*upasarga*).
The *Kātyāyana-śruti* states: "In the beginning, middle, or end of a word, and likewise when joined with a *ṛ*-vowel, the same rule applies even in the case of doubling.
Furthermore, for the second of the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), there should be an utterance accompanied by the vowel *e*.
With the consonants *ha*, *la*, *bha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and when joined with the vowel *ṛ*—
and likewise for the third [consonant] when joined with *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*— one should perform the pronunciation with the vowel *e*; such is the established rule of the scriptures.
One should pronounce the letter *ṛ* with the vowel *e* added to it from all sides, whether it is joined or unjoined; the same applies to the letter *l*.
Furthermore, at the end, the final [syllable] is pronounced in three ways: as heavy, medium, and light.
In a sentence, the initial, middle, and final [syllables], as well as those at the beginning and end of a word, should be understood as light;
however, in a mantra, *vaḥ*, *vām*, and *vai* are to be known as light, while in a *pada* they are heavy.
Examples for "devo vaḥ savitā" and other such cases should be sought elsewhere.

The pronunciation of *kh* after a non-conjunct *m* followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) is considered [the rule]; however, even when *s* is conjunct with *m*, that very same conjunction applies. In Vedic meter (*chandas*), the pronunciation of *kh* is desired as the worldly natural form (*prakṛti*).

In the Vedic language (chandas), it is traditionally taught that the anusvāra is replaced by the syllable *aṃ*. When followed by sibilants (*ūṣman*) or *r*, its triple articulation (*traividhya*) is prescribed:
after a short vowel, it is long; after a long vowel, it is short; and when followed by a heavy syllable (*guru*), it is heavy.
When followed by the letter *ṛ*, a spirant at the end of a word may become long even after a long vowel;

for in the case of *parasavarṇa*, the anusvāra is said to have a very slight natural form. The anusvāra has the measure of a minute atom (*aṇu*), and the final [nasal] also has the measure of a minute atom.

Where there are the letters śa, ṣa, sa, ka, kha, pa, and pha, or where there is a visarga, there a pause in speech should be made because of the injunction of the *iṣacchruti*. This is understood to apply to the letter 'a' that is joined [with another consonant] or which stands at the beginning of a word. (18–19)

The recitation [of the name] should be performed with slight lengthening according to the word of the sage Kātyāyana; [this work] was composed by Keśava, the son of Daivajña Gokula, who was born in the lineage of that orthodox sage, for the sake of attaining auspiciousness. 20.1–2.1b.
For the delight of the wise, this pure and auspicious *Kārikāvalī* has been composed. 21.
